node.label: Digital history
node.description: Historical research, interpretation, preservation, teaching and public communication using digital media. This overlaps with quantitative, computational and public history without being equivalent to any of them or to all digital humanities.
node.scope_note: Partial entry draft, not a founding chronology or comprehensive field survey through 2026. Older breadth-packet works remain separate research and must be reconciled before acceptance.

representative_people.context: Leon criticizes Thomas’s digital-history genealogy for omitting women historians. Leon’s specific critique; Thomas’s chapter has not been independently read in this batch. The AHR authors report expanding their account after reading Leon’s intervention. Authors’ documented acknowledgement during revision, not proof of field-wide influence or a date for final publication. Leon links exclusions in digital-history narratives to academic status, institutional location and the invisibility of collaborative labour. Selected chapter paragraphs, US-focused argument; her grant tallies are not independently reproduced here or adopted as this graph’s demographic baseline.
representative_people.works: Complicating a “Great Man” Narrative of Digital History in the United States

representative_people.context: Gallini and Noiret frame digital history around research, communication, preservation and teaching, and ask how digital media change historical practice. Spanish original pp. 16–17; English paraphrase. This Colombian dossier is an intervention, not proof of one Latin American consensus or a founding date. Gallini and Noiret connect digital historical communication to collaborative design and translation between historical and technical expertise. Spanish original pp. 17–18; a programme for collaboration, not an attribution of all technical work to historians or a claim that digital history replaces older inquiry.

node.label: Web history / Archived-web research
node.description: Historical inquiry into the web and inquiry using archived web evidence. These overlap but differ: web archives also inform political, social and cultural histories whose object is not the web itself. Archival and information scholars contribute contextual methods without being assigned an exclusive historian profession.

representative_people.context: Hegarty attributes gaps and uneven access in Australian social-media archives to different collection strategies and changing platform constraints. Indexed author abstract only; two Australian library cases. No detailed findings beyond that abstract, and no claim that all national archives behave alike. Hegarty explicitly adapts Ann Stoler’s attention to archival form and placement to interpreting platform-mediated web collections. Indexed author abstract only; specifically attributed methodological use, not a general Stoler-to-web-history influence arrow or a new reading of Stoler’s book.
representative_people.works: Web archives after platformization: reading social media collections along the archival grain

representative_people.context: Gibbons presents mediated recordkeeping and platform paradata as ways to document how archival processes shape evidential meaning. Selected introduction/conclusion. The model originated in earlier doctoral research; the 2026 paper presents a diagnostic framework, not a field-tested institutional implementation. Gibbons argues that making archival gaps visible cannot itself redistribute authority or settle Indigenous sovereignty and community-governance questions. Selected limitations/conclusion; a stated boundary of the model, not a claim that technical documentation delivers justice or substitutes for Indigenous-led decisions.
representative_people.works: Mediated recordkeeping and epistemic accountability in social media archiving
